subject: zoology
question_text: Mention the general characters of Arachnida.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.36, SAQ 29). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: What the arachnids are
steps.why: The chelicerates are named after their first pair of appendages, so the absence of antennae follows from the name of the subphylum itself.
common_mistakes: Giving them a head, thorax and abdomen. The arachnid body has two parts, prosoma and opisthosoma.
Giving them antennae. No chelicerate has antennae.
steps.memory_tip: Two body parts and no antennae: prosoma in front, opisthosoma behind.
steps.margin_note: Class, subphylum, habitat, body divisions. Four or five lines.
lines: Arachnida is a class of chelicerate
arthropods. Its members are mostly
terrestrial.
The body is divided into two parts: the
prosoma in front and the opisthosoma behind.
Antennae are absent, as in every chelicerate.

steps.label: Appendages
steps.why: The count six is fixed for the class, and it is the four pairs of walking legs at the end of that list that separate an arachnid from an insect with three pairs.
common_mistakes: Giving three pairs of walking legs. Three pairs belong to insects; arachnids have four pairs.
Placing the spinnerets on the prosoma. They are modified appendages of the opisthosoma.
steps.memory_tip: Six pairs: chelicerae, pedipalps, then four pairs of legs. Four pairs, not three.
steps.margin_note: List the six pairs as a, b, c. Then one line on the spinnerets.
lines: The prosoma carries six pairs of appendages:
a) one pair of chelicerae
b) one pair of pedipalps
c) four pairs of walking legs.
The spinnerets of a spider are modified
abdominal appendages. They give out the silk
the spider spins its web from.

steps.label: Organ systems
steps.why: Haemocyanin carries copper where haemoglobin carries iron, which is why arachnid blood is not red.
common_mistakes: Naming haemoglobin. The arachnid pigment is haemocyanin, and it holds copper.
Giving only one excretory organ. Both Malpighian tubules and coxal glands are named.
steps.memory_tip: Copper pigment, not iron. Book lungs on land, tracheae in some spiders.
steps.margin_note: Respiration, pigment, excretion. One line each.
lines: Respiration is by book lungs, as in the
scorpion, and by tracheae in some spiders.
The respiratory pigment is haemocyanin,
which contains copper.
The excretory organs are the Malpighian
tubules and the coxal glands.

steps.label: Development and examples
steps.why: The young hatch already shaped like the adult, so no larval stage is needed, and in the scorpion they are carried until then inside the mother.
common_mistakes: Writing that arachnids have a larval stage. Development is direct.
Writing that scorpions lay eggs. Scorpions are viviparous.
steps.memory_tip: No larva at all, and the scorpion gives birth to live young.
steps.margin_note: Development, then the scorpion's habit, then the examples.

lines.text: Two body parts · Six pairs on the prosoma

lines: Development is direct. There is no larval
stage.
Scorpions are viviparous. They give birth to
young ones.
Examples:
Palamnaeus — the scorpion.
Aranea — the spider.
Sarcoptes — the itch mite.

insider_note: Four pairs of walking legs is the line that most often separates a correct arachnid answer from an insect answer written by mistake.
